utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I notice -- recognise that General Talic is not here. Has the registrar -- has the registrar received any communication as regards his absence?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, I have not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Andrew Cayley, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman along with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Ackerman and the rest. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning to you. Do you have any communication as regards your client to make to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would assume that we should go into the closed session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just before that happen, I think we need confirmation that General Talic is content the hearing goes ahead as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it ought to be done in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I mean by "communication" is precisely that. Because the rest will come out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there the consent of your client, not being present today, to proceed in his absence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we have a consent of our client to proceed today without his being present in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Is there any objection forthcoming from the Prosecution or any one of the Defence teams that we go into closed session for a while? Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. There's -- no. In fact, the suggest was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For a while, because it's an interim decision, which will be reconsidered as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, we've suggested all along that it should be -- in fact we made other suggestions that it should be even more private, but we're happy, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Madam Registrar, please can we go into closed session for a while until further instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose we can start. I understand we're going to start with the motion of General Talic, regarding the part of the testimony of Mr. Filipovic relating to the events experienced in Stara Gradiska military camp. And I give the floor to Mr. Zecevic -- or Madam Fauveau, yes. Please try to restrict your submissions to about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we will discuss it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I'll be very brief, because our arguments are in fact very simple. This Tribunal rendered a decision on the 23rd of November, 2001 and refused to the Prosecutor amendment of the indictment and refused to have facts introduced in this indictment, facts that have been committed in Stara Gradiska. The reason for this decision, according to the Chamber, is that none of the Prosecutor's allegation in the indictment establishes connections between General Talic and the events that took place outside of the territory of Bosnia. This decision was confirmed by your order, Mr. President, of the 8th of December, 2001, in which you judged that the indictment -- that the Prosecution is not competent to judge about an event that took place in the prison -- in the military prison in Stara Gradiska. It is our opinion that the pre-trial phase has reasons to exist in order to clarify the indictment and to allow the accused to be familiar with facts with which he is reproached and to ensure the expeditious proceedings. And during the pre-trial proceedings, this problem was a subject of two decisions, two identical decisions, and I think that this is a matter that was ruled upon, and to allow the Prosecutor today to introduce events concerning Stara Gradiska would mean allowing the Prosecution not to respect the decisions of this Tribunal, and this would result in a lack of respect for the judicial procedure before this Tribunal. I think that the Prosecution wants to introduce events relating to 1 the distinction that this Tribunal makes in its case law between facts that 2 have to be included in the indictment and evidence that shouldn't be 3 included. It is true that the case law of this Tribunal makes this 4 difference. Nevertheless the evidence has to concern the alleged facts in the indictment and only the facts alleged in this indictment. The Prosecutor pretends that he does not reproach General Talic with the events in Stara Gradiska. It is a matter of fact that show the general context. We don't agree with this argument for a simple reason: According to the Prosecution's arguments, the 5th Corps allegedly had under its command the Stara Gradiska area, and General Talic was the commander of the 5th Corps. Given this situation, in fact, the Prosecution reproaches General Talic with what took place in Stara Gradiska and considers him responsible for what took place in Stara Gradiska. Defence cannot allow these facts to be introduced in this case because Defence is not in a position to and is not prepared to respond to these facts. These facts are not included in the indictment, and in addition they are the subject of a decision of the Tribunal which rejected, which didn't allow the Prosecutor to introduce these facts in the indictment. And given this case, I don't think that there is a reason for me to expand on this debate, and I don't think that we should allow the Prosecutor to obtain a decision which would be contrary to the decision which has already been rendered by this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. I, too, will be very brief. As you know and as, I think, Ms. Ivanovic has made clear, there are no specific charges within the indictment relating to the events at the Stara Gradiska prison, and we readily acknowledge that. But from the outset, and referring to your decision, Judge Agius, of the 7th of December, 2001, and in reading the -- I think it's about the fourth paragraph. It states that "The Prosecution would not be entitled to rely upon any events alleged to have occurred at the Stara Gradiska military prison." We would argue that that particular part of the order relates to specifically relying on those events to sustain a specific charge within the indictment. We acknowledge that Talic would not be held directly criminally responsible for the events in Stara Gradiska. However, having said all of that, the events which took place in Stara Gradiska are an integral part of the account and the story of a number of witnesses who were forcibly transferred or deported out of the Krajina region and onto the Manjaca camp. Stara Gradiska was a stopping-off point for them where crimes were committed, as Mr. Filipovic, I think, indicated in his evidence, and a number of witnesses were transferred in this manner. And in my submission, it would be an inaccurate portrayal of the evidence to you if we were to, as it were, cut out a portion of a witness's testimony that is relevant to understanding the entire context in which all of these crimes took place and to, as it were, interfere or tamper with a witness's evidence of his account, his story of what happened to him during this time period. Secondly in respect of the matter as to whether or not the accused General Talic was on notice of the events in Stara Gradiska. By virtue of the indictment, by virtue of the evidence, he was on notice that Stara Gradiska was a part of this case because witness statements were disclosed to him which referred to peoples, individual, witnesses passing through this particular camp. So he was aware of that. He did -- he did know that evidence would be led in respect of Stara Gradiska camp. I think it's also worth mentioning to you Rule 93 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which I'm not sure if you have that in front of you. Rule 93 is a rule which envisages "Evidence of a consistent pattern of conduct relative to serious violations of international humanitarian law, under the Statute, may be admissible in the interests of justice. Acts tending to show such a pattern of conduct shall be disclosed by the Prosecutor to the Defence pursuant to Rule 66." It's clear that what happened in Stara Gradiska is evidence of a consistent pattern of serious violations of international humanitarian law that were taking place in the Krajina, with which this case is principally concerned, and that those acts were disclosed to General Talic under Rule 66 by virtue of the witness statements that were transmitted. And we would argue that even if this evidence cannot be directly relied upon by the Prosecutor to sustain charges - and we acknowledge that - it is evidence of a consistent pattern of conduct across the Krajina region, which we would argue should be admissible in the interests of justice. Ultimately, Your Honours, you are professional Judges. There is no jury here. You have the experience and the expertise to give this evidence the weight that it deserves. It may not deserve the weight of evidence which specifically relates to charges with which General Talic himself has been charged, but it may well be evidence that you believe in the interests of justice should be considered within the overall context of what took place in this region in 1992. That would be my submission. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, would you like to reply with regard to the submission made by Mr. Cayley to the Rule -- which number? Rule 93.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'll be very brief once more. I think that it would be in the interest of justice for the accused to be well aware of what he's being charged with, and it would be in the interests of justice for the decisions to be respected, as far as Rule 93 is concerned. This is exactly what I wanted to say earlier on. The events in question aren't events that can show that the accused -- the accused's behaviour within a general context, because these are events that took place outside the territory which is in the indictment. This territory requires special investigations. The territory in question is a very complicated territory. It consists of the Republic of Croatia, the Serbian Republic of Croatia and the United Nations. Without knowing exactly that these facts would be in the indictment, I don't see why the Defence should have to spend money and time on investigating this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could I add one last thing. And it is a matter which my learned friend actually acknowledges in her own motion. We say, in the evidence that we disclose, that Stara Gradiska was the headquarters of the 5th Corps, subsequently the 1st Krajina Corps, from December of 1991 to June of 1992. It was General Talic's forward headquarters, that was co-located with this particular camp. If we're talking about evidence, the matters that she's referred to. That is a matter for you on the merits of evidence, but nevertheless that is something that has been disclosed. So it's not some far flung place that we have suddenly introduced into the evidential tapestry. That is a fact. And a number of prisoners, a number of individuals who were detained in Manjaca will testify that they passed through Stara Gradiska on the way to Manjaca. So I would only add those points, Your Honour, in terms of the evidence itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anything else? Any further submissions? Mr. Ackerman, do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, only that I join in the motion of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any further submissions?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We should be in a position to hand down an oral decision shortly. We need to talk a little bit. We did discuss the system of conduct yesterday in chambers, amongst ourselves. I think we need to discuss a little bit further and then we will be able to hand down the decision later on, either later on today or first thing tomorrow morning before -- before we start, whatever. Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know you don't like apologies. But just the reason for my delay was the case -- the other case I was involved in actually went on. And I thought you wanted to start earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, I'm not dealing with children. I know that you are starting from Ms. Korner, right down to the least in the hierarchy, that you have been extremely responsible. So I do not doubt your -- you don't need to. When I will have reason, which I hopefully never have, to censor anyone one of you or to demand an apology, I will not hesitate. But until now, I don't. Certainly not. Neither your team nor any of the Defence teams, either of the Defence teams. So that, having been said, can we go into -- we don't need to. Mr. Zecevic, in preparation for what we will need -- what we will be doing at -- starting from half 12.00, I would require from you on behalf of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A specific declaration releasing the witness and any further witnesses from professional secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay? You understand why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because this is no longer a merit of the piece of paper that we had in front of us this morning. We're going deeper into that. And if there are additional persons coming forward, as there may be, I also want to know that your client is prepared to waive any of his rights, as regards access to third parties, to whatever information they may require to be able to assist this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. And I will take the necessary measures to inform my client and get the instructions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I -- is there anything else we can do now before -- All right. So then I suppose we can reconvene five minutes before half 12.00, and hopefully we should be in a position to hand down the decision on Stara Gradiska. So we'll start in open session first. We'll start in open session first, and then we'll continue in closed session. All right? Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.38 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the Stara Gradiska. We have concluded our discussions in camera, the three Judges, and we are agreed completely on what decision to hand down, and it will be an oral decision, but I would rather prefer to hand it down tomorrow morning rather than now because I would still prefer to have some points jotted down before I start pronouncing our decision. So tomorrow morning, first thing, please expect the decision. Now, I think what we're going to discuss now will require us to go into closed session once more. So my apologies to the members of the public. It's a delicate moment, delicate issue that we have to discuss which is strictly personal to one of the accused and therefore we need to go into closed session. So Madam Registrar, could we go into closed session, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (redacted)b

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.58 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of September, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
